function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

{"output": "## Chapter One: The Shock

### Summer 1958, Northern Michigan

The summer of 1958 arrived in Michigan like all the others before it—warm, languid, scented with pine and lake water. For six-year-old Bob, this summer marked something else entirely: the precise moment when memory begins, crystalline and sharp, or so he would come to believe.

The family had traveled north to a modest cabin nestled among the woods, a ritual escape from the sweltering heat of the lower peninsula. Bob's father had secured some time away from work, no small feat in those years, and the family packed themselves into the car with the practiced efficiency of people who had learned to make do with little. The cabin was simple—wooden walls, a small kitchen, bedrooms that smelled of cedar and mothballs—but to a child of six, it contained universes of possibility.

On this particular afternoon, the adults had retreated to the front room, their voices a low murmur of adult conversation that signaled safety and boredom in equal measure. Bob was alone in the kitchen, a space transformed by his solitude into something approaching a laboratory—full of drawers to open, cabinets to explore, and mysteries yet undiscovered.

His father's car keys lay on the counter, abandoned in the transition from arrival to settling in. They were ordinary keys, the kind any man might carry in 1958, but they bore an adornment that captured Bob's complete attention: a Native American puzzle fob. The fob was intricate, a small wooden object carved with geometric precision, its pieces interlocking in ways that suggested both order and mystery to a curious young mind.

Bob picked up the keys. The metal felt cool against his palm. He turned the fob over and over, studying the way the pieces fit together, wondering at the cleverness of whoever had designed such a thing. His fingers traced the carved surfaces, finding the slight ridges where tool had met wood.

But childhood curiosity is a restless thing, never satisfied with a single mystery when another might lie nearby. As Bob twisted the puzzle fob, his eyes wandered upward, scanning the kitchen walls until they found what they sought: an electrical outlet.

Bob knew about electrical outlets. He had heard the warnings—parents in 1958 were no less vigilant about such dangers than they are today, perhaps more so in an era before ground fault interrupters and child-safety covers. The words had been spoken: "Don't put things in the outlet." But words are abstract things to a six-year-old, weightless concepts that lack the gravity of experience. The allure of the outlet was not defiance, exactly. It was something more primal—the same impulse that sends children to poke sticks into streams, to peer down wells, to press their faces against aquarium glass. The outlet was a mystery. The keys were in his hand. And in the mind of a curious child, these two facts began to form a question that demanded an answer. What would happen?

The memory, if memory it is, plays out with the slowness of a dream. Bob gripping the key—not the fob end, but the metal shaft. His small hand extending toward the outlet. The twin slots waiting, dark and silent and full of promise.  What happened next would become the foundational moment of Bob's life, the first chapter in a story that would unfold across seven decades. The key made contact.

Electricity is invisible. We see its effects—light, heat, motion—but the current itself remains hidden, a ghost in the walls. In that moment, six-year-old Bob met this invisible force directly, unfiltered, raw.  The shock surged through his body with the indifference of physics acting upon matter. His muscles contracted involuntarily, a puppet's dance with invisible strings. The force threw him backward—"catapulted," he would later think of it, though at six he possessed no such vocabulary. He flew several feet across the kitchen, landing in a heap against the far wall.

Darkness. Not the gentle dark of bedtime, but a violent absence of sight. His heart hammered against his ribs like something trying to escape. His hand—oh, his hand—tingled with a strange, persistent vibration that seemed to echo the current that had passed through it. Time dilated. Those agonizing moments of disorientation stretched into what felt like hours, though they were likely only seconds. Bob sat in a daze, grappling with the reality of what had just occurred. His body had touched something invisible and been punished for it. The world had revealed one of its hidden rules.

Then came the footsteps—hurried, panicked. His parents burst into the kitchen, their faces transformed by concern and confusion. They found their son crumpled against the wall, the keys lying on the floor between him and the outlet, the connection obvious even without explanation.  The scolding came, as scoldings do. Words of admonishment, expressions of fear dressed in anger. Bob was told what he already knew, what his body had learned in the most direct way possible: electricity was dangerous. The warnings, so abstract before, had found their weight. And yet…

Here is where the memory, if memory it is, takes an unexpected turn. Despite the terror of the moment, despite the scolding that followed, six-year-old Bob felt something else entirely. The experience was terrifying, yes, but it was also—exhilarating. The shock had been a revelation. In touching that outlet, Bob had reached beyond the ordinary boundaries of childhood into a realm of invisible forces and physical laws. He had asked a question of the universe—what will happen?—and the universe had answered with unmistakable clarity. The pain was real. The fear was real. But so too was the learning, immediate and visceral, in a way that no textbook or parental warning could ever achieve.  This was science. This was discovery. This was the moment when a child realizes that the world operates according to principles that can be tested, that cause leads to effect with mathematical precision, that even the most dire warnings cannot compare to the power of direct experience.

### The Memory of Memory

But here we must pause. Because Bob, looking back across sixty years from the vantage of the present, can never be entirely certain that this memory belongs to him. The mind is a trickster. Cognitive psychologists have established this with certainty: every time we recall a memory, we reconstruct it. The act of remembering alters the memory itself, like a document being retyped with slight variations each time. Details shift. Emotions intensify or fade. The boundary between what actually happened and what we believe happened becomes porous, permeable, eventually indistinguishable. Bob's mother told the story of the electrical outlet many times as he grew up. She would recount it at family gatherings, using it as a cautionary tale for younger cousins, shaking her head at her son's reckless curiosity. With each retelling, the story gained texture—Bob's fascination with the puzzle fob, the exact sound of his body hitting the wall, the expression on his father's face when he entered the room.  Did Bob remember these things? Or did he remember his mother remembering them? The memory he carries feels real—the tingling hand, the taste of fear, the strange exhilaration that followed. But feeling real and being real are different things. A false memory can feel as vivid, as certain, as one formed from actual experience.

### The Science of Uncertainty

This uncertainty—the impossibility of knowing whether the memory is genuine or constructed—would haunt Bob throughout his life. It became a lens through which he examined all his recollections, a nagging doubt that colored every "I remember when." Was his memory of that first day of school authentic? His memory of his grandfather's voice? His memory of anything? The memories that shaped his personality, his fears, his desires—how many of them were borrowed from photographs, from stories, from the collective mythology of family? From his own foggy memories? The electrical outlet incident, real or reconstructed, became the cornerstone of Bob's "memory palace"—the mental architecture where he stored his most significant experiences. But unlike other memories that gradually clarified with age, this one remained stubbornly ambiguous. It existed in a quantum state, simultaneously real and imagined, its truth dependent entirely on the observer.

### The Spark That Ignited

What is not ambiguous is the effect this event had on the course of Bob's life. Whether he actually felt that jolt of electricity or merely believed he had, the result was the same: an awakening. The experience ignited something in Bob—a fascination with electricity that would evolve into a passion for science and technology. In the months and years that followed, he devoured books on electrical circuits with the hunger of someone who had tasted the power hidden in walls and wished to understand it. He conducted home experiments, some dangerous, all illuminating. He built gadgets from scrap parts, learning through trial and error the principles that governed the invisible force that had once thrown him across a kitchen. His parents, perhaps recognizing that his curiosity could not be extinguished—only channeled—nurtured his scientific endeavors. They bought him books. They tolerated the mess of his experiments. They learned to check the fuse box after he had been "working" in the basement. This passion led to academic excellence in science, which led to university, which led to degrees in electrical and systems engineering. The little boy who had touched the outlet grew into a man who would help design systems for NASA, who would contemplate missions to Mars, who would spend his professional life facing toward the stars.

### The Metaphor

But the gift of the electrical outlet incident was not merely vocational. It was philosophical. The memory—if memory it is—taught Bob something fundamental about the nature of knowledge. It taught him that understanding requires risk, that the pursuit of truth sometimes demands that we touch the very things we're warned against, that learning is not always safe or comfortable. It taught him about the malleability of memory itself. His uncertainty about the authenticity of the experience led him to study the neuroscience of recollection, to understand concepts like "reconsolidation" and the construction of false memories. He learned that human memory is not a video recording but an active, creative process—a story we tell ourselves about ourselves, subject to revision with each telling. Most importantly, it taught him that the most formative moments of our lives might be partly—or entirely—fictional, and yet remain no less powerful for it. Whether Bob actually touched that outlet and felt that shock matters less than the fact that he believes he did, that this belief shaped his curiosity, his career, his very identity.

### The Loop

Now, as Bob stands in his seventh decade looking backward through the telescope of time, the electrical outlet incident remains his earliest memory—or his earliest believed memory. It sits at the foundation of everything that followed, the first domino in a cascade that created the man he would become. He has studied the brain since then. He knows about synaptic plasticity and long-term potentiation. He understands that memories form when neurons fire in patterns, strengthening their connections through repetition and emotional significance. He knows that strong emotions—like the fear and wonder of that moment in the kitchen—create particularly vivid memories, etched deep into the hippocampus and the amygdala. But knowing the mechanism does not resolve the mystery. Bob still cannot say with certainty whether he remembers the shock itself or only remembers his mother telling him about it. The memory remains stubbornly dual, existing in two states at once, a quantum superposition of real and imagined. Perhaps that is fitting. Perhaps the ambiguity itself is the lesson—the recognition that our pasts are not fixed things but ongoing creations, stories we revise as we age, meanings we make from events that may or may not have occurred exactly as we recall them.

### The Beginning

So this is where we begin: with a six-year-old boy in a Michigan cabin, holding his father's keys. With a moment of curiosity that crossed a boundary. With a shock that may or may not have happened exactly as remembered, but that changed everything regardless. The outlet still waits in the wall of memory, dark and full of promise. The key still hangs in the air, metal gleaming, poised between innocence and experience. The child still sits on that far kitchen floor, heart pounding, hand tingling, eyes wide with the terror and wonder of discovery. Whether it happened or not, it is true. It is the creation myth of a life, the spark that lit a flame that still burns sixty years later. It is the first chapter of a story about memory and identity, about how the past creates the present creates the future in an endless loop of becoming. The shock was literal, perhaps. Or it was metaphorical. Or it was both. But its effect was undeniable. It launched a boy across a kitchen and into a life of inquiry, a life spent reaching toward mysteries just beyond the fingertips, trusting that the answers—even when they shock us—are worth the seeking. In the end, it doesn't matter whether Bob remembers that day or only remembers remembering it. The memory has done its work. It has shaped a human being who would spend his life questioning, exploring, wondering—who would never accept that the walls contain nothing more than wires, who would always suspect that just behind the ordinary surface of things lies something extraordinary, waiting to be touched. *The outlet waits. The key turns. The story begins.*

That electrical spark—the literal shock and the metaphorical awakening it ignited—would have to wait for its perfect complement when something far more distant than a kitchen outlet began to beep its way across the night sky. ## Chapter One: The Shock

### Summer 1958, Northern Michigan

The summer of 1958 smelled like pine sap and lake water, like cedar shingles baking in the heat and the faint mothball ghost of a cabin that had been closed up too long. I was six years old, and if I'm being honest—if I'm being *true*—that summer marks the precise moment my memory clicks on. Everything before it is fog and family story. Everything after is mine.

We'd driven up from lower Michigan, my father at the wheel, my mother navigating with the quiet competence that defined her. The cabin was nothing special: wooden walls, a linoleum floor in the kitchen, bedrooms that smelled of closed windows and old blankets. But to a six-year-old, it was an undiscovered continent. Every drawer held a mystery. Every cupboard concealed a treasure.

On that particular afternoon, the adults had drifted to the front room. Their voices were a low murmur, the sound of safety, of boredom, of the strange currency of grown-up conversation. I was alone in the kitchen, and that kitchen had become my laboratory.

My father's car keys lay on the counter. They were ordinary keys—the kind any man carried in 1958—but they wore a puzzle fob that seemed to me a piece of art. A small wooden carving, Native American in design, interlocking geometric pieces fitted together with a precision that demanded investigation. I picked up the keys. The metal was cool against my palm. I turned the fob over and over, tracing the carved ridges where a craftsman's tool had met the wood, wondering at the cleverness of whoever had made such a thing.

But childhood curiosity is a hungry animal. It cannot be satisfied long by one mystery when another waits nearby.

As I twisted the fob in my small fingers, my eyes wandered the kitchen walls until they found what they sought: an electrical outlet. Twin slots, dark and silent, mounted in the wood paneling like a question mark without a curve.

I knew the warnings. Every child in 1958 knew the warnings. "Don't put things in the outlet." My mother had said it. My father had said it. It was a rule, as fixed and unquestioned as the rule about not running into the street. But rules are abstract things to a six-year-old. They're words without weight, language without experience. The outlet was a mystery. The keys were in my hand. And in the mind of a child, those two facts began to circle each other like planets finding orbit, forming a question that demanded an answer.

*What would happen?*

---

I remember gripping the key shaft. I remember my hand extending toward the outlet, a small astronaut reaching toward a new world. I remember the twin slots waiting, dark and full of promise.

The key made contact.

Electricity is invisible. We see its fingerprints—light, heat, motion—but the current itself hides behind walls, a ghost we've learned to domesticate. In that moment, I met that ghost directly, unfiltered, raw. The shock surged through my body with the indifferent authority of physics acting upon matter. My muscles clenched. My arm locked. The force threw me backward—catapulted me, I'd later think, though at six I had no such word for it. I flew across the kitchen and landed in a heap against the far wall.

Darkness. Not the gentle dark of sleep, but a violent absence—a blink of the universe. My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped thing. My hand—*oh, my hand*—tingled with a strange, persistent vibration, the echo of the current that had passed through it. Time became elastic. Those moments of disorientation stretched into something that felt like hours, though they were surely seconds. I sat on that linoleum floor, dazed, my body having learned something that all the warnings in the world could never teach.

Then came the footsteps. Hurried. Panicked. My parents burst into the kitchen, their faces transformed—my mother's eyes wide, my father's jaw set. They found me crumpled against the wall, the keys on the floor between me and the outlet, the story written clearly enough without a single word spoken.

The scolding came, as scoldings do. Words of admonishment dressed in fear, delivered in tones that betrayed how close they had come to something worse. I was told what I already knew, what my body had just learned in the most direct way possible: electricity was dangerous. The warnings, so abstract before, had found their weight.

And yet.

Here is the part that still surprises me, seventy years later. Despite the terror. Despite the scolding. Despite the tingle that lingered in my hand for hours afterward—I felt exhilaration. The shock had been a revelation. In touching that outlet, I had reached beyond the ordinary boundaries of childhood into a realm of invisible forces and physical laws. I had asked a question of the universe—*what will happen?*—and the universe had answered with unmistakable clarity. The pain was real. The fear was real. But so too was the learning, immediate and visceral, in a way no textbook or parental warning could ever achieve.

This was science. This was discovery. This was the moment a child realizes the world operates according to principles that can be tested, that cause leads to effect with mathematical precision, that even the most dire warnings cannot compare to the power of direct experience.

### What I Remember vs. What I Was Told

But here we must pause, because I cannot be entirely certain this memory belongs to me. The mind is a trickster, a master forger of its own past. Cognitive science has proven this beyond doubt: every time we recall a memory, we reconstruct it. The act of remembering alters the memory itself, like a document retyped with slight variations each time. Details shift. Emotions intensify or fade. The boundary between what happened and what we believe happened becomes porous, permeable, eventually indistinguishable.

My mother told the story of the electrical outlet many times as I grew up. She would recount it at family gatherings, using it as a cautionary tale for younger cousins, shaking her head at her son's reckless curiosity. With each retelling, the story gained texture—my fascination with the puzzle fob, the exact sound of my body hitting the wall, the expression on my father's face when he entered the room. Did I remember these things? Or did I remember *her* remembering them?

The memory I carry feels real. I can feel the cool metal of the key. I can hear the crackle of electricity. I can taste the ozone in the air afterward. But feeling real and *being* real are different things. A false memory can be as vivid, as certain, as one formed from actual experience. I have studied the neuroscience since then. I know about synaptic plasticity and long-term potentiation. I understand that strong emotions—like the fear and wonder of that moment in the kitchen—create particularly vivid memories, etched deep into the hippocampus and amygdala. But knowing the mechanism does not resolve the mystery. I still cannot say with certainty whether I remember the shock itself or only remember my mother telling me about it.

And perhaps that is fitting. Perhaps the ambiguity is itself the lesson.

### The Spark That Lit a Life

What is *not* ambiguous is the effect this event had on the course of my life. Whether I actually felt that jolt of electricity or merely believed I had, the result was the same: an awakening. The experience ignited something in me—a fascination with electricity that would evolve into a passion for science and technology that has spanned seven decades.

In the months and years that followed, I devoured books on electrical circuits with the hunger of someone who had tasted the power hidden in walls and wished to understand it. I conducted home experiments—some dangerous, all illuminating. I built gadgets from scrap parts, learning through trial and error the principles that governed the invisible force that had once thrown me across a kitchen. My parents, perhaps recognizing that my curiosity could not be extinguished—only channeled—nurtured my scientific endeavors. They bought me books. They tolerated the mess of my experiments. They learned to check the fuse box after I had been "working" in the basement.

That passion led to academic excellence in science, which led to university, which led to degrees in electrical and systems engineering. The little boy who touched the outlet grew into a man who would help design systems for NASA, who would contemplate missions to Mars, who would spend his professional life facing toward the stars. The creation myth of a life: a six-year-old boy, a kitchen outlet, and a question that demanded an answer.

The gift of that moment was not merely vocational. It was philosophical. It taught me that understanding requires risk, that the pursuit of truth sometimes demands we touch the very things we're warned against, that learning is not always safe or comfortable. It taught me that the most formative moments of our lives might be partly—or entirely—fictional, and yet remain no less powerful for it. Whether I actually touched that outlet and felt that shock matters less than the fact that I *believe* I did—that this belief shaped my curiosity, my career, my very identity.

The outlet still waits in the wall of memory, dark and full of promise. The key still hangs in the air, metal gleaming, poised between innocence and experience. The child still sits on that far kitchen floor, heart pounding, hand tingling, eyes wide with the terror and wonder of discovery. Whether it happened or not, it is true. It is the first chapter of a story about memory and identity, about how the past creates the present creates the future in an endless loop of becoming.

That electrical spark—the literal shock and the metaphorical awakening it ignited—would have to wait for its perfect complement. Because something far more distant than a kitchen outlet was about to begin beeping its way across the night sky, and the child who had touched invisible forces in a Michigan cabin was about to discover that the universe held reaches extending far beyond anything he could yet imagine.
